{{short description|Result used in the theory of propagation of waves}}
The '''Sommerfeld identity''' is a mathematical identity, due [[Arnold Sommerfeld]], used in the theory of [[Wave propagation|propagation of waves]], 

:<math>
\frac{{e^{ik R} }}
{R} = \int\limits_0^\infty I_0(\lambda r) e^{ - \mu \left| z \right| } \frac{{\lambda d \lambda}}{{\mu}}
</math>

where
:<math>
\mu = 
\sqrt {\lambda ^2  - k^2 } 
</math>
is to be taken with positive real part, to ensure the convergence of the integral and its vanishing in the limit <math> z  \rightarrow \pm \infty </math> and
:<math>
R^2=r^2+z^2
</math>.
Here, <math>R</math> is the distance from the origin while <math>r</math> is the distance from the central axis of a cylinder as in the <math>(r,\phi,z)</math> [[cylindrical coordinate system]]. Here the notation for Bessel functions follows the German convention, to be consistent with the original notation used by Sommerfeld. The function <math>I_0(z)</math> is the zeroth-order [[Bessel function]] of the first kind, better known by the notation <math>I_0(z)=J_0(iz)</math> in English literature.
This identity is known as the Sommerfeld identity in radial-spectral form.{{sfn|Sommerfeld|1964|p=242}}

In alternative notation, the Sommerfeld identity can be more easily seen as an expansion of a spherical wave in terms of cylindrically-symmetric waves:{{sfn|Chew|1990|p=66}}
:<math>
\frac{{e^{ik_0 r} }}
{r} = i\int\limits_0^\infty  {dk_\rho  \frac{{k_\rho  }}
{{k_z }}J_0 (k_\rho  \rho )e^{ik_z \left| z \right|} } 
</math>
where
:<math>
k_z=(k_0^2-k_\rho^2)^{1/2}
</math>
The notation used here is different from that above: <math>r</math> is now the distance from the origin and <math>\rho</math> is the radial distance in a [[cylindrical coordinate system]] defined as <math>(\rho,\phi,z)</math>. The physical interpretation is that a spherical wave can be expanded into a summation of cylindrical waves in <math>\rho</math> direction, multiplied by a two-sided [[plane wave]] in the <math>z</math> direction; see the [[Jacobi-Anger expansion]]. The summation has to be taken over all the wavenumbers <math>k_\rho</math>.

The Sommerfeld identity is closely related to the two-dimensional [[Fourier transform]] with cylindrical symmetry, i.e., the [[Hankel transform]]. It is found by transforming the spherical wave along the in-plane coordinates (<math>x</math>,<math>y</math>, or <math>\rho</math>, <math>\phi</math>) but not transforming along the height coordinate <math>z</math>. {{sfn|Chew|1990|p=65-66}}

== Axial-spectral representation of the Sommerfeld identity ==
The radial forms above integrate over the transverse spectral variable λ (equivalently <math>k_\rho</math>), which leaves the axial dependence to appear through a two-sided exponential in <math>z</math>. A complementary form rather integrates over the axial wavenumber <math>k_z</math>, keeping the axial phase explicit and expressing the transverse dependence through a cylindrical (Hankel) wave{{sfn|Chew|1990|p=66}}:

<math>\frac{e^{ik_0R}}{R}=\frac{i}{2}\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}H_0^{(1)}(k_\rho \rho)e^{ik_z z} dk_z,
\quad k_\rho = \sqrt{k_0^2-k_z^2},\ \text{Im}(k_\rho)\geq 0,</math>

where <math>\rho</math> is the radial distance in the cylindrical system <math>(\rho, \phi, z)</math>, <math>R = \sqrt{\rho^2+z^2}</math>, and <math>H_0^{(1)}</math> is the [[Hankel function]] of zeroth-order of the first kind. The branch of <math>k_\rho</math> is chosen such that <math>H_0^{(1)}(k_\rho \rho)</math> is representative of an outgoing wave for <math>k_z^2 < k_0^2</math> and is evanescent for <math>k_z^2 > k_0^2</math>, which ensures convergence.{{sfn|Chew|1990|p=66}}

This form is obtained via the same spherical wave by transforming along thew axial coordinate <math>z</math> alone, instead of along the in-place coordinates. This representation is used in spectral-domain analyses of cylindrical structures and layered media, where the <math>e^{ik_zz}</math> factor allows axial and transverse operations to be separate, and where the Hankel-function argument makes the two-centre translation of cylindrical waves tractable (via Bessel-family addition theorems, for example).
